waitReasons.letter: I'm waiting for a letter, for example the ELSTER activation letter
waitReasons.ask: I need to ask someone first
waitReasons.decide: We have to decide this internally

12_1.headline: Find out whether and how NIS 2 applies to you
12_1.teaser: Sector and size decide the level.
missed: If more than one type of entity applies, record every one, not just your main line of business.
If your company belongs to a group, partner and linked enterprises count towards headcount and turnover. That does not apply if your IT demonstrably runs independently of them (§ 28(4) BSIG).
Side activities that hardly matter to your business as a whole may be left out of the assignment (§ 28(3) BSIG).

learn.title: Whether NIS 2 applies to you
body: NIS 2 applies to companies in certain sectors above a certain size. The sectors are listed in two annexes to the BSI Act. A company that falls under it is either an essential or an important entity.
There is no official notice for this. The law decides who is covered, and you check it yourself.
learn.duty: Whether and at which level your company is covered follows from its sector and its size.

thresholds.title: Size is part of it
thresholds.lead: What counts is headcount, or turnover and balance sheet together. The higher threshold applies only to sectors in Annex 1.
thresholds.source: § 28(1) no. 4 and (2) no. 3 BSIG. For some types of entity size does not matter, for example operators of critical facilities.

data.title: What you need for it
data.lead: The figures are usually in your latest annual accounts.

items.name: Employees
items.detail: how many people work for you

items.name: Annual turnover and balance sheet total
Your activities
items.detail: how your company earns its money, to compare with Annexes 1 and 2

items.name: Holdings
items.detail: whether your company belongs to a group

data.source: § 28(4) BSIG refers to Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC for the counting. For a first orientation the BSI offers the online NIS-2-Betroffenheitsprüfung; according to the BSI its result is not legally binding.

classification.title: Record your classification
classification.lead: Two details. Management confirms them with its signature at the end.

done.title: Classification recorded
done.note: If your size or your lines of business change, check the classification again.

applicableSectors.label: Sectors and types of entity
applicableSectors.hint: Every one that applies to your company, with its number from Annex 1 or 2 of the BSIG, for example 1.1.1 for electricity suppliers.

1_1.headline: Get management trained
missed: The training should cover the goals of § 38(3) BSIG: recognising and assessing risks and risk management, and judging what they mean for your company's services.

The law says "regularly" and names neither an interval nor a duration. The BSI recommends a thorough first training followed by refresher trainings, with duration and interval set by your risk exposure.

learn.title: Training for management
body: Whoever runs the company takes part in information security training regularly. This applies to every member of management personally.
You will find a course for this on this platform. You can also choose any other provider; the law does not require providers to be accredited.
learn.duty: Management has to take part in training regularly. How often and for how long, the law does not say.

record.title: What a record can look like
record.caption: Write down who learned what, and when:

rows.name: Content
rows.detail: recognising and assessing risks, effects on our services

training.title: Record the latest training
training.lead: Who gave it and when. If there has not been one yet, enter it once it has taken place.

certificates.title: One record per person
certificates.lead: File the certificate of attendance for every member of management.

done.title: Training recorded
done.note: At the end, management reviews every item and signs.

managementTrainingProvider.label: Training provider
managementTrainingProvider.hint: Who gave the training, for example a training institute, a consultancy or an online course.

lastManagementTraining.label: Date of the latest training
lastManagementTraining.hint: The date on the certificate of attendance.

5_1.headline: Write down who works for you
5_1.teaser: A list of your suppliers and service providers.
missed: IT is not the only thing that counts. The law speaks of direct suppliers and service providers without restriction (§ 30(2) no. 4 BSIG).
The EU Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) suggests classifying suppliers, for example as critical, strategic and routine.

learn.title: Who works for your company
body: Security also covers whoever works for you from outside: service providers, software vendors, suppliers. The first step is a list of who they are and what they do for you.
Start with the ones your business could not run without. The list grows over time.
learn.duty: The law requires measures for supply chain security, including in your relationships with your direct suppliers and service providers.

list.title: What your list can look like
list.caption: One line per supplier, with what they do for you:

rows.name: IT provider
rows.detail: looks after servers and accounts, has remote access

rows.name: Microsoft
rows.detail: email and files for all staff

sources.title: Where the names already are
sources.lead: Your company usually knows its suppliers already. Tick where you have looked:

suppliers.title: Your suppliers
suppliers.lead: Enter each one and say how important it is to your business. When in doubt, write it down rather than leave it out.

dependence.title: Who could stop you on their own
dependence.lead: How many suppliers are there without whom your business would stop, and for whom no second one is ready?

done.title: Your list is in place
done.note: When a supplier comes along, add it. At the end, management reviews the list.

singlePointOfFailureCount.label: Number of such suppliers
singlePointOfFailureCount.hint: Count the entries where a failure stops your business and there is no replacement.

payables.label: Accounts payable list
payables.text: From accounting. Whoever sends you invoices works for you.

contracts.label: Contracts and subscriptions
contracts.text: Maintenance contracts, software licences, cloud accounts.

provider.label: Your IT provider
provider.text: They know which vendors they use on your behalf.

12_3.headline: Keep the registration up to date
12_3.teaser: When something changes, update it with the BSI.
missed: The two weeks run from the moment your company learns of the change. So add the BSI portal to what happens when someone leaves the company.
Give a shared mailbox for the point of contact, as the BSI recommends. Then less changes.

learn.title: Keep the details up to date
body: When something changes in what you gave the BSI at registration, update it in the BSI portal, under "Ihre Registrierung".
The law does not require a fixed yearly check. It requires you to be quick when something changes.
learn.duty: Report changes without undue delay, and at the latest two weeks after your company learned of them.

changes.title: When to update

items.name: Contact person and point of contact
items.detail: someone leaves or takes on a different job

items.name: Address, phone and email
items.detail: a move, a new number, a mailbox switched off

items.name: Public IP address ranges
items.detail: a new internet connection or a new provider

items.name: Sector and EU member states
items.detail: a new line of business or services in another country

changes.source: § 33(1) and (5) BSIG. Changes are made in the BSI portal under "Ihre Registrierung" (BSI guide).

contact.title: Who is registered with the BSI
contact.lead: So you know whom the BSI reaches, and notice when that person leaves.
contact.document: Your registration in the BSI portal

done.title: Contact recorded
done.note: At the end, management reviews every item and signs.

contactPersonName.label: Contact person
contactPersonName.hint: The person entered in the BSI portal as the NIS 2 contact person.

contactPersonEmail.label: Contact person's email address
contactPersonEmail.hint: As it appears in the BSI portal.

lastRegistrationUpdate.label: Last updated
lastRegistrationUpdate.hint: The day you last changed the details in the BSI portal. Leave it empty if nothing has changed yet.

1_2.headline: Decide who takes care of it
1_2.teaser: One coordinating role, with a deputy.
missed: In its NIS 2 checklist the BSI recommends at least two people for the coordinating role. Then it is covered during holidays or illness too.
The person needs direct access to management at any time, to report incidents and risks (BSI Standard 200-2).
The role does not have to be called CISO. The BSI calls it the information security officer (Informationssicherheitsbeauftragte, ISB).

learn.title: Who takes care of it
body: Management carries the responsibility. It has to implement the measures and oversee their implementation (§ 38(1) BSIG). It hands the work to people in the company.
At the centre is one coordinating role. It drives information security forward and advises management.
learn.duty: Your company has to document how it meets its duties. That includes who is responsible for what.

good.value: Ms Kaya from commercial management, with Mr Brandt as deputy, both with a direct line to management
good.note: Two people, close to the top. That is what the BSI recommends.

bad.note: If they are out, nobody takes care of it. And whoever runs the systems then judges their security themselves.

roles.title: Enter the roles
roles.lead: Who coordinates, who deputises and who decides in an incident.

done.title: Roles assigned
done.note: At the end, management reviews every item and signs.

3_1.headline: Plan what happens in an incident
3_1.teaser: Who decides, whom you call, how you reach each other.
missed: Plan a second way to communicate outside your own IT. The law explicitly names secured communication and, where needed, secured emergency communication (§ 30(2) no. 10 BSIG).
Decide who writes the report to the BSI. The first report is due at the latest 24 hours after you learn of a significant incident (§ 32(1) BSIG).

learn.title: When something happens
body: During an incident there is no time to work out who does what. So write it down beforehand: who decides, whom you call, and how you reach each other when email and the network are down.
It does not have to be a thick manual. One page that everyone can find is enough to start with.
learn.duty: The law requires your company to be able to handle security incidents.

lead.title: Who leads in an emergency
lead.lead: One person decides, a small team helps.

escalation.title: Whom you call
escalation.lead: Who gets told when, from IT up to management.

second_way.title: The second way
second_way.caption: How you reach each other when email and the network fail

good.value: A phone list on paper, at the office and at management's homes
good.note: Works even when your own IT is down.

bad.note: If email itself is affected, the message never arrives.

channel.title: Your second way
channel.lead: How you reach each other when your own IT is not working.

plan.title: File the plan
plan.lead: Upload your emergency plan, even if it is only one page. Management approves it.

done.title: Plan recorded
done.note: At the end, management approves the plan with its signature.

incidentLead.label: Incident lead
incidentLead.hint: The person who decides what to do and informs management.

irtTeamSize.label: Team size
irtTeamSize.hint: How many people work on it in an emergency, including external ones such as your IT provider.

incidentEscalationContacts.label: Escalation contacts
incidentEscalationContacts.hint: Names and phone numbers, by severity of the incident. Include your IT provider's emergency number.

secureCommsChannel.label: Second communication channel
secureCommsChannel.hint: A way outside your own IT, for example a phone list on paper.

3_3.headline: Know how to report an incident
3_3.teaser: Three reports to the BSI, with fixed deadlines.
missed: The clock runs from when you learn of it, not from when everything is clear. Report early; the second report confirms or updates the first.
The BSI reads "learning of it" as the moment someone in the company finds out about the incident during working hours.
If personal data is affected, report to the data protection authority in parallel, with its own 72-hour deadline (Art. 33 GDPR).

learn.title: Reporting an incident
body: If a security incident is significant, you report it to the BSI. It is significant if it can seriously disrupt your operations or cause you financial losses, or if it can cause considerable damage to others.
Reports are made in the BSI portal, with the same access as for the registration.
learn.duty: You report significant incidents in three steps to the joint reporting office of the BSI and the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance.

clock.title: The three deadlines
clock.lead: The clock runs from the moment your company learns of the incident. The third deadline starts with the second report.
clock.source: § 32(1) and (2) BSIG. If the incident is still going on after a month, send a progress report instead of the final report, and the final report once it is dealt with.

deadline.title: Your deadline for the first report
deadline.lead: The law sets this number. You only confirm it.
deadline.source: § 32(1) no. 1 BSIG: without undue delay, and at the latest within 24 hours of becoming aware.

ready.title: What you need for the first report
ready.lead: Settle this now, not in the middle of an emergency:

items.name: Access to the BSI portal
items.detail: you have it since the registration

items.name: Who reports
items.detail: one person and a deputy, written into the emergency plan

items.name: What you know
items.detail: what is affected, since when, and whether an attack could be behind it

ready.source: § 32(1) no. 1 BSIG. A company that is not registered yet reports through the BSI's reporting and information portal (BSI, Meldepflicht info pack).

done.title: Reporting prepared
done.note: At the end, management reviews every item and signs.

earlyWarningSlaHours.label: Deadline for the early warning, in hours
earlyWarningSlaHours.hint: At the latest 24 hours after your company learns of a significant incident.

12_2.headline: Register with the BSI
12_2.teaser: Your company registers with the BSI once.
missed: The BSI asks for all of your company's public static IP address ranges (§ 33(1) no. 2 BSIG). Your IT provider knows them. Ask them beforehand. If you have none, say so.
A new organisation certificate needs an activation letter that comes by post. According to Mein Unternehmenskonto this takes at least five working days. Apply early.

learn.title: Registering with the BSI
body: Every company NIS 2 applies to registers once with the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI). You tell the BSI who you are and how to reach you.
This is done online in the BSI portal. You log in with "Mein Unternehmenskonto" and an ELSTER organisation certificate. If your company already has one, for example from tax filings, use that one.
learn.duty: Registration is a duty of its own. It is due no later than three months after your company counts as an important or essential entity.

data.title: What the BSI asks for
data.lead: The law requires these details. Have them ready before you open the portal.

items.name: Name and legal form
items.detail: with the commercial register number, if you have one

items.name: Address and contact details
items.detail: email address, phone numbers and your public IP address ranges

items.name: Sector
items.detail: from Annex 1 or 2 of the BSIG, with the subsector where one applies

items.name: EU member states
items.detail: in which your company provides these services

items.name: Supervisory authorities
items.detail: those at federal and state level responsible for your activity

data.source: § 33(1) BSIG. The portal also asks for a point of contact and a contact person (BSI registration guide).

contact.title: What good looks like
contact.caption: The email address you give the BSI

good.note: A shared mailbox, as the BSI recommends in its guide. People move on, the mailbox stays.

bad.note: A personal address. If Ms Müller changes jobs, the BSI reaches nobody.

confirmation.title: Record the registration
confirmation.lead: Two details, so you know later which certificate was used and on which day.
confirmation.document: Your access to the BSI portal

proof.title: File a proof
proof.lead: In the BSI portal, the overview of registered procedures (registrierte Fachverfahren) lists every completed registration. A screenshot or a printout of that page records that yours is done.

done.title: Registration recorded
done.note: At the end, management reviews every item and signs.

mukAccountId.label: User account ID of the organisation certificate
mukAccountId.hint: Every ELSTER organisation certificate carries its own number, the Benutzerkonto-ID. Whoever manages the certificate can tell you.

bsiRegistrationDate.label: Date of registration
bsiRegistrationDate.hint: The day someone clicked "Registrierung abschließen" (complete registration) in the BSI portal.

2_1.headline: Decide how you rate risks
2_1.teaser: The BSI has a ready-made method for this.
missed: Attacks are not the only thing that counts. The law requires an all-hazards approach (§ 30(2) BSIG). The EU directive explicitly requires protecting the physical environment of the systems too (Art. 21(2) NIS 2), for example against fire, water or a power cut.
Which risks are accepted is decided by management, as BSI Standard 200-3 also provides. Record that limit with a date.

learn.title: How you rate risks
body: Before you write down risks, decide how you rate them. Then everyone in the company rates them by the same rules.
The BSI has a ready-made method for this, Standard 200-3. Every risk gets two ratings: how often can it happen, and how big would the damage be? Together they give one of four levels.
learn.duty: The law requires concepts for risk analysis. It does not prescribe a particular method.

matrix.title: The BSI's matrix
matrix.lead: Across: how often something happens. Down: how big the damage would be. Where the two meet is the level.
matrix.source: BSI Standard 200-3, Figure 3. The BSI presents it as an example and says it should be adapted to the individual needs.

reading.title: How to read the matrix
reading.caption: A server goes down once a year to once a month. The damage is limited and manageable.

adopt.title: Adopt the method
adopt.lead: One click records the method. This is how it will then appear in your records:

lines.label: Method
lines.text: Risk analysis according to BSI Standard 200-3

lines.label: Levels
lines.text: Four for frequency, four for damage, four risk levels

lines.label: Matrix
lines.text: The assignment from Figure 3 of the standard

acceptance.title: Which risks your company accepts
acceptance.lead: Up to which level may a risk remain without you doing anything about it? Management decides this. Choose the proposal here that management signs at the end.
acceptance.source: In its examples, BSI Standard 200-3 assumes that an organisation "accepts 'Low' risks as a matter of principle, but 'Medium', 'High' and 'Very high' risks only in exceptional cases".

done.title: Method set
done.note: At the end, management reviews the method and the limit and signs.

2_2.headline: Write down what your company has
2_2.teaser: A list of the processes, software and devices you work with.
missed: Software you rent from the cloud belongs on the list too, for example email or accounting.
For processes and applications, the BSI expects a responsible person (Standard 200-2, section 8.1). Note who knows each one.

learn.title: What your company works with
body: You can only protect what you know. So write down what your company works with: processes, information, software, devices, rooms and networks. The BSI calls this step the structure analysis (Standard 200-2, section 8.1).
The list does not have to be perfect. When something new comes along, add it.
learn.duty: The law requires concepts for risk analysis and for managing your IT systems, products and processes. Both start with this list.

list.title: What your list can look like
list.caption: Short is fine. One line per thing:

sources.title: Where your list already exists
sources.lead: The BSI advises looking for existing overviews. Tick where you have looked:

processes.title: What your company does every day
processes.lead: Tick what runs at your company. When in doubt, write it down rather than leave it out.

business_apps.title: Software for customers, staff and money
business_apps.lead: What you use to serve customers, pay wages and keep the books.

shared_apps.title: Software everyone uses
shared_apps.lead: Email, file storage, chat and anything only your industry has.

technology.title: Technology and rooms
technology.lead: Servers, devices, network and the places where people work.

protection.title: How many protection levels you use
protection.lead: A protection level says how bad it would be if something failed, was altered or got out.

done.title: Your list is in place
done.note: When something new comes along, add it at any time. At the end, management reviews the list.

classificationLevels.label: Number of protection levels
classificationLevels.hint: The BSI works with three levels: normal, high and very high (Standard 200-2, section 8.2.1). Choose a different number only if your company already classifies differently.

ropa.label: Record of processing activities
ropa.text: From data protection (Art. 30 GDPR). It describes what you process personal data for, and often names the software too.

ledger.label: Fixed asset register or inventory list
ledger.text: From accounting. It lists devices and other equipment your company has bought.

provider.label: Your IT provider
provider.text: They know your servers, accounts and cloud services.

12_1.who: Compliance or legal gathers sector, headcount and turnover. Management confirms the classification: with it, it decides which duties the company takes on.
12_1.ask: Are we an essential or an important entity, and which entity types from Annex 1 and 2 apply to us?
missed: Several sectors: the main one is not the only one that counts. Record every entity type that applies.

Groups: each company is classified on its own. Data of partner enterprises counts pro rata and of linked enterprises in full, unless the company's own IT demonstrably runs independently of them (§28(4) BSIG).
Negligible side activities may be left out of the classification (§28(3) BSIG). Re-check the classification after growth, new lines of business or acquisitions.

12_2.who: Compliance or legal requests the organisation certificate and enters the details in the BSI portal. IT supplies contact details and public IP ranges. Management reviews the details before they are submitted.
12_2.ask: Are we registered with the BSI, and when were the registered details last checked for accuracy?
missed: Access runs through an ELSTER organisation certificate (Mein Unternehmenskonto). An existing certificate, for instance from tax filings, can be used; a new one arrives by post with an activation letter. Apply early.
Public IP ranges are part of the mandatory details (§33(1) Nr. 2 BSIG). Ask IT beforehand, or the registration stalls at this point.
Register a functional mailbox as the contact, not a personal one. People change; the reporting office must still reach someone.

1_1.who: Every member of the management body in person. The duty in §38(3) BSIG rests on management itself; nobody can attend on their behalf. IT or information security selects the content, HR or compliance archives the records.
1_1.ask: Has every member of the management body taken part, and does the record show content, duration and date?
missed: The training has to cover the learning goals in §38(3) BSIG: identifying and assessing risks, assessing risk management practices, and judging their impact on the company's own services.

The law sets neither an interval nor a minimum duration, only "regularly". Set your own rhythm and write down the reasoning. A change in the management body or a clearly changed risk situation is a trigger outside the calendar.
The record counts, not the provider: capture participants, content, duration and date. There is no accreditation requirement for training providers.

2_1.who: Information security (the ISB or CISO) picks the method and sets the scales. Management decides how much residual risk the company carries: that threshold is its decision, not IT's.
2_1.ask: Show me the risk matrix and the top right corner. What is our threshold for acceptable risk, and did I approve it?
missed: All-hazards means more than cyber. §30(2) BSIG requires an all-hazards approach, and Art. 21(2) NIS 2 explicitly requires protecting the physical environment of the systems too, for example against fire, water or a power cut.
The acceptance threshold is often never set explicitly. It belongs in the methodology as a dated management decision of its own, not buried in the risk register.
The threat landscape is part of the method: name a source of current threat intelligence, at minimum the BSI situation reports.

2_2.who: Every row has an owner in the business who knows the system and keeps the entry current. Information security consolidates the inventory and checks the protection needs. IT supplies the technical details, data protection flags systems holding personal data.
2_2.ask: Show me the inventory. When was it last updated, and are cloud services and external access in it?
missed: Every asset needs an owner. A list without that column does not survive an audit.
Cloud, SaaS and third-party access are assets. So is operational technology in production and buildings (OT), which brings requirements of its own.
The GDPR record of processing activities (RoPA, Art. 30) is a good starting stock: many systems are already listed there.

5_1.who: Procurement, or whoever holds the contract, adds the supplier. Information security rates risk and criticality, legal reviews the contract clauses. Management knows the list of critical suppliers.
5_1.ask: Which suppliers could halt our operations or have access to our systems, data or premises, and who on our side is responsible for each of them?
missed: Not only IT suppliers: §30(2) Nr. 4 BSIG speaks of direct suppliers and service providers without qualification. Anyone who can disrupt operations belongs in the register.
Every row needs an owner and a rating. Without both, the register is a list of names in an audit.
Subcontractors do not end at the first link. For critical services, ask whom the supplier relies on in turn.

12_3.who: Compliance or legal reviews the registered details and reports changes. IT and information security speak up when contact details or IP ranges change.
12_3.ask: Who at our company learns of a change of contact person, address or sector, and who updates it with the BSI?
missed: The deadline is short: changes without undue delay, at the latest within two weeks of becoming aware of them (§33(5) BSIG). An annual check alone is not enough.
The data goes stale quietly: the contact person leaves, the mailbox is switched off. A functional mailbox and an item in the leaver process prevent that.

1_2.who: Information security drafts who carries which task. Management appoints the person responsible for information security and approves the division of tasks. Legal checks the lines of authority, HR supplies the org chart.
1_2.ask: Who is responsible for information security here, does that person report directly to me, and have I seen the division of tasks for the remaining measures?
missed: The role does not have to be called CISO. What matters is one person who is responsible for information security towards management; BSI Standard 200-2 calls this role the information security officer (ISB).

An ISB placed under the head of IT is a conflict of roles: whoever runs the systems should not be the only one judging their security. BSI Standard 200-2 provides for a direct reporting line to management.
Data protection officer and ISB in one person: then write down where one role ends and the other begins.

3_1.who: Information security writes the plan and names the lead of the incident team. Legal or compliance drafts the notification texts, data protection covers incidents involving personal data. Management approves the plan.
3_1.ask: Who decides whether an incident is significant? By which route and from which threshold does the escalation reach me, and when did we last test the fallback communication channel?
missed: A second communication channel outside your own IT. In a real incident, email and chat are often affected too; §30(2) Nr. 10 BSIG names secured emergency communication explicitly.
Detecting is not handling. Monitoring without a defined response, ownership and escalation is not a plan.
Whoever drafts the report to the BSI is rarely in the plan. Fill that role in advance; in smaller companies it sits with compliance or legal.

3_3.who: Information security classifies the incident and clears the report, compliance or legal drafts it, IT supplies the facts. Management is informed without delay. Data protection checks in parallel whether the supervisory authority has to be notified (Art. 33 GDPR).
3_3.ask: Who decides what counts as significant, and when did we last exercise the reporting route, in a real incident or a drill?
missed: Three reports, one incident: an early warning within 24 hours, a notification within 72 hours, and a final report one month after the second report (§32(1) BSIG). If the incident is still ongoing, a progress report takes its place (§32(2) BSIG).
The recipient is the joint reporting office of the BSI and the BBK. Reports are filed through the BSI portal with the same access used for registration.
If personal data is affected, the notification to the data protection authority under Art. 33 GDPR runs in parallel, with its own 72-hour deadline.
